schools.summary: Gill refuses the indictment on both counts: Job had uttered nothing vain enough to be compared with wind, and the fear in question is the grace of fear, a covenant blessing that can never be lost.

Henry turns first on the speaker, since proud men take it amiss when they may not dictate to all about them, and then grants the general truths about vain knowledge and idle words that the charge is built on.

Clarke makes the east wind the stormy wind of the Levant, so that Job's speech is a tempest of words, and hears the old serpent in the tongue of the crafty; Wesley calls such discourse pernicious, not merely unprofitable.

Keil and Delitzsch open the second course of the controversy with Eliphaz as the most influential of the three, reading Job's answers as impassioned tirades; Ellicott reduces the charge to the bare claim that Job is not wise.

debates.issue: How far Eliphaz's indictment of Job can be allowed

positions.view: Gill denies both charges outright, the second on the doctrinal ground that saving fear is a gift without repentance.
Ellicott allows that Job's tendency to fatalism would in fact check prayer and set a dangerous example.
Henry calls the construction unjust but not wholly without colour, and faults the friends for provoking the words they now use against him.

themes: Eliphaz opens the second round
vain knowledge and the east wind
casting off fear and restraining prayer
the tongue of the crafty
a man condemned by his own mouth
1.pericope_label: Should a wise man utter vain knowledge: thine own mouth condemneth thee

schools.summary: Gill concedes only that a deceitful heart sometimes carries away even good men, and that if this was Job's case at all it was owing to his own heart.

Henry answers the appeal to antiquity by noting the oldest are not always the wisest, and charges Eliphaz with wanting candour, since to construe a tempted man's words so is in effect to give the cause on Satan's side.

Clarke reads the sarcasm as asking whether Job was born before Adam, identifies the grey-headed with Eliphaz and his two companions, catalogues eight renderings of the verse on God's consolations, and makes the winking eye the furious rolling of a deranged man.

Ellicott treats the opening as a retort on Job's earlier claim and calls the consolations verse very difficult to decide; Keil and Delitzsch supply the assumption that the first man had the profoundest insight, and render the spirit turned against God as snorting.

debates.issue: Whether the verse on the consolations of God can be settled

positions.view: Clarke lays out eight renderings, observes that scarcely any two translators agree even on the meaning, and leaves the reader to choose.
Ellicott calls it very difficult to decide and lists further possibilities, while Keil and Delitzsch simply decide for the promises made in accordance with God's majesty, spoken in a gentle tone.

outliers.view: That Eliphaz's construction of Job's words was in effect to give the cause on Satan's side, and to own that Job had done what Satan said he would.

themes: Art thou the first man that was born
the secret of God
the appeal to grey hairs and antiquity
the consolations of God
a spirit turned against God
7.pericope_label: Art thou the first man that was born: why doth thine heart carry thee away

schools.summary: Gill renders the noun woeful man, says the question is put by way of contempt to abate a man's conceit of himself, and takes the holy ones for sanctified men whom God trusts with much but never with themselves.
Henry presses the use being made of a true doctrine, since Job had said the same thing two chapters earlier, and holds that a man not clean as born of a woman is clean as born again of the Spirit.

Clarke argues that the particle should be rendered how much less rather than how much more, cites the Vulgate for the sense that among God's saints none is immutable, and sets the bad man who thirsts after sin against the good man who thirsts after righteousness; Wesley takes the holy ones for angels, pure from corruption but not from imperfection.
Ellicott notes that this is the ceaseless burden of the book, and that language so strong in general terms is meant to reflect on Job.

debates.issue: Who the holy ones are in whom God puts no trust

positions.view: Wesley and Clarke take them for the angels, many of whom fell, all their goodness being derived and dependent.
Gill takes them for sanctified men, whom God trusts with His messages but not with their own preservation.
Henry allows both and keeps the comparative force of the argument.

debates.issue: Whether the particle means how much more or how much less

positions.view: Clarke holds that since God puts no trust in His holy ones the sense must be how much less would He confide in man.
Henry, working from the received text, reaches the same sense by the parallel that if the heavens are not pure, much less man, who is degenerated.

themes: What is man, that he should be clean
the holy ones and the heavens
how much more or how much less
drinking iniquity like water
a doctrine Job had already granted
14.pericope_label: What is man, that he should be clean: how much more abominable is man

schools.summary: Gill states the thesis being defended, that only wicked and not righteous men are afflicted of God, and argues that the men to whom the earth was given cannot be the patriarchs but are more likely Noah and his sons.

Henry notes how apt men are to commend their own reasoning while condemning another's, defends both the observing of providences and the transmitting of what the ancients knew, and answers the taunt by denying that those who are impoverished are therefore not God's people.

Clarke takes the favoured men for the Israelites and judges the whole collection of ancient sayings good in itself but sinfully misapplied to Job; Wesley presses the insinuation that God would have warded off every enemy from Job too, had Job been such a one.

Keil and Delitzsch mark that the dogma now rests on observation and tradition rather than on the revelation of the first speech; Ellicott notes that the appeal to the fathers borrows the language of another of the friends.

debates.issue: Who the men were to whom alone the earth was given

positions.view: Clarke takes them for the Israelites, who received the promised land from God with no stranger permitted to dwell in it.
Gill objects that the patriarchs did not yet enjoy the land, and reads it of Noah and his sons, among whom the whole earth was divided.

outliers.view: That the wise sayings Eliphaz is about to quote are all good enough in themselves, but sinfully misapplied to the case of Job.

themes: I will shew thee, hear me
experience and the tradition of the fathers
the earth given to the favoured alone
no stranger passed among them
prosperity as evidence of standing with God
17.pericope_label: I will shew thee, hear me: that which wise men have told from their fathers

schools.summary: Gill divides the pain between the labour of iniquity, the sorrows of keeping wealth and the gripes of conscience, adds that it cannot be said of every wicked man, and turns the dreadful sound on Job, whose troubles arrived by one messenger after another.
Henry traces the terror to conscience, which shows the sinner a flaming sword turning every way and himself running upon it, and asks what the hell before him is if this be the hell within him.
Clarke makes the man a self-tormentor and sole author of his own ruin, doubts that the darkness means the grave, and quotes the poet that few usurpers go down to the shades by a dry death.

Keil and Delitzsch render the verb as writhing in inward distress; Ellicott corrects the division of the sentence, judges the portrait overdrawn in places, and leaves the man the tennis-ball of calamity.

debates.issue: Whether the darkness he will not return from is the grave

positions.view: Gill allows the sense of the infidel without hope of a glorious resurrection, laid in the dark and silent grave.
Clarke doubts it, holding that a future judgment was understood wherever the knowledge of the true God had reached, and keeps the plainer sense of the assassin's dagger.

themes: the wicked man travaileth with pain
a dreadful sound in his ears
no return out of darkness
wandering abroad for bread
trouble and anguish as a king ready to battle
20.pericope_label: The wicked man travaileth with pain: trouble and anguish shall make him afraid

schools.summary: Gill has the wicked man run upon God with a stretched-out neck, as the he-goat of the vision ran upon the ram, and reads the desolate cities as ruins of his own making, rebuilt greater to perpetuate his name.

Henry presses the absurdity, that a sinner out of God's reach still stretches out his hand as though he would ungod him, and gets two things from the fat that covers him, a bold face and a soft life that will prove poor shelter against the darts of God's wrath.

Clarke follows Calmet in making God the one who rushes upon the ungodly and seizes him by the throat, reports an Arabic proverb about laying the Pleiades on the Hyades for boundless ambition, and counts six threatened evils all aimed at Job; Wesley calls it the madness of a poor worm that dared fight the omnipotent God.

Ellicott reassigns the shield from God to the wicked man's own prosperity, which has blinded him; Keil and Delitzsch deny that the desolate cities are his ruins at all, reading a careless security without fear of God's judgments.

debates.issue: Who runs upon whom in the clause about the thick bosses of the shield

positions.view: Gill makes the wicked man the assailant, grappling with God as a warrior takes his antagonist by the throat.
Clarke, following Calmet, reverses the subject: God marches against the ungodly like a conquering hero, and the mail cannot protect the throat He seizes.
Ellicott keeps the wicked man as subject but holds it less probable that the armour is God's, making it the man's own prosperity.

debates.issue: Whose ruins the desolate cities are

positions.view: Gill, with Henry, makes them cities he destroyed himself and then rebuilt or emptied so as to dwell alone in them.
Clarke makes the ruins his punishment, a tyrant obliged to lodge in a city his own wars had wrecked.
Keil and Delitzsch deny they are his ruins, since the verb points to an appointed future, and read a powerful man settling down without fear of judgment.

themes: stretching out the hand against God
the thick bosses of the shield
a face covered with fatness
dwelling in desolate cities
he shall not be rich
25.pericope_label: He stretcheth out his hand against God: the flame shall dry up his branches

schools.summary: Gill traces the deceiving to Satan, to a man's own heart and to the deceitfulness of sin, distinguishes a death before a man's own expected term from one before the term fixed in God's decree, and thinks Eliphaz has his eye on Job's own household.

Henry makes the mischiefs that befall others our warning against leaning on a broken reed, and names malice and falsehood as the stock in trade of him who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning.

Clarke says flatly that Job is here classed with hypocrites and accused of taking bribes, and closes with the sufferer himself, whose enemies were all chained and could not go beyond that chain; Wesley reads the recompense as an exchange of one vanity for another.

Ellicott catches Eliphaz throwing Job's own uncommon word for desolate back at him, and judges the peroration to be only the familiar maxim that the wicked are punished in this life, which fails utterly against afflictions like Job's; Keil and Delitzsch make the family of the ungodly a lifeless stony mass.

debates.issue: Whether the closing argument proves anything against Job

positions.view: Ellicott holds that the speech only repeats the orthodox maxim that the wicked are punished in life, a maxim which fails in the face of Job's afflictions unless he was one of the wicked.
Clarke reads the last verses as two direct insinuations against Job, of hypocrisy and of bribery, and answers them by pointing to the chain on all his enemies.

outliers.view: That the rare word for desolate was Job's own, so that there may be an intentional reference to his use of it.

themes: let not him that is deceived trust in vanity
cut off before his time
the unripe grape and the olive flower
the congregation of hypocrites
they conceive mischief and bring forth vanity
31.pericope_label: He shall not be established: they conceive mischief and bring forth vanity
